prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned Romanian-language prose and poetry that turn memory, the body and dream into an inner cosmos of metaphysical and historical reach.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: one writer, B050, Mircea Cărtărescu. I reassessed it against the chair's round-2 questions and not against the fact that all six round-1 files name him, which is not evidence of merit. The claim rests on four criteria. First, voice: the long, hallucinatory, densely patterned prose is recognizable at once. Second, formal achievement: Blinding (the first part of the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid, on public knowledge, are built as large architectures in which recurring images and structures carry the meaning. Third, intellectual depth: the work joins the single consciousness, the body and dream with cosmological speculation and the history of twentieth-century Romania. Fourth, breadth: the writer began as a poet and also writes essays, so the claim covers an oeuvre. In answer to the chair's question about which works I rely on, my case rests mainly on Blinding and Solenoid. The poetry, essays and earlier prose support it only as context, and I say so openly. My citation wording now names the Romanian language, as Sem-Sandberg's round-1 wording did. That keeps the language of the achievement explicit, so the citation does not imply a claim for the translations. It changes the wording only, not the laureate or the scope. On the chair's last question, I see no merit or citation ground to hold back from B050 or to prefer P000 this year. I cannot fully test the central reservation, whether the late volumes deepen the project or repeat it, from public knowledge. I do not think that gap alone makes the no-award option the better choice. A single-writer citation raises no attribution problem. This rests on public knowledge, not fresh reading or independent verification.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unresolved, and I do not treat it as settled. The same scale and density that make the work distinctive may turn into self-enclosure, encyclopedic accumulation or repeated motifs across the late volumes. If that were shown, the sustained-quality and maturity criteria would be weaker than I have assumed. The evidence also reaches us through translation, which only partly conveys the rhythm and syntax of long Romanian sentences. The poetry, essays and early prose are the least covered part of the corpus, so part of the whole-oeuvre claim is inferred from the major novels. Round 1 produced no close-reading evidence that resolves any of this. The consensus on B050 is therefore only as strong as these open questions, and I would weigh a specific, evidenced argument about repetition more heavily than any count of support.

responses.point: Olsson moved from Zurita first in his opening to Cărtărescu first, and keeps Zurita as his first alternative. He now treats the translation exposure of the poetry, the non-textual interventions and the single sequential project as more consequential than he first allowed. He also stresses that any Zurita citation must be limited to the written poems.
responses.response: I agree that a Zurita citation would have to be worded strictly around the written sequences (Purgatory, Anteparadise), with the landscape interventions treated only as an extension. That is also why I keep B009 as my first alternative and not as a rival first choice. The voice and the moral and formal seriousness are real. What I cannot establish from the translated corpus is whether the poems stand on their own in Spanish, apart from their historical occasion. I note that your shift came from weighing exactly that asymmetry between what can be assessed and what is suspected. I think that is the honest ground for it. I also take your point that repetition applies to both of our leading candidates. If the committee had a reliable Spanish-language reading showing that the sequences develop and do not circle, I would give Zurita far more weight.

responses.point: Sward keeps Cărtărescu first and names repetition in the very large late volumes as the most serious qualification on her own choice. She argues the cycles should be judged as a whole and not by the late volumes alone. She ranks Tawada second as a linguistic and formal case that works at shorter scale, and now names B009 among her alternatives.
responses.response: I accept that the cycles should be judged as wholes, and I rely on Blinding and Solenoid in that way. I do not claim the late volumes alone settle the question. On Tawada, I did not rank her in my opening. The estrangement she builds between Japanese and German is a serious formal idea, and I cannot weigh it fairly against the work I know better. Your own doubt, whether short and episodic forms carry the depth of a whole authorship, is the question I would want answered. Evidence that her shorter pieces accumulate into a developing project, and not a sequence of well-made variations, would strengthen her case. It might also change which alternatives I name. For now I would not place her above B009 or B039 on what I can actually assess.

responses.point: Mattson keeps NDiaye as an alternative. She values the controlled, uncanny voice and the added range from drama. She acknowledges that the oeuvre is more compact than the largest on the list. In round 2 she was asked to specify which NDiaye works carry the main claim across decades.
responses.response: In round 1 I asked which works you see as carrying the claim, and I think that remains the decisive question for NDiaye. Three Strong Women and My Heart Hemmed In are the books I know best, and they show the economy and tonal control you describe. A whole-authorship prize needs evidence that the later novels and plays deepen that method and do not only repeat it. I accept that compactness is not a defect in itself, and I do not hold it against her. My reservation is narrower. Syntax and register shifts are what translation flattens most, and the drama is least covered abroad. I ranked her fifth, and my view has not moved. I would revise it if you can show a developmental arc across her decades of work.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg asked that the Yan Lianke case be kept separate from restriction in China and rest on the formal invention of mythorealism. He now names B009 as an alternative. He also asks the committee to test directly whether Cărtărescu's excess is imaginative depth or a lack of selection.
responses.response: I agree with both requests. For Yan Lianke, The Four Books and The Explosion Chronicles are formally inventive, and the grotesque and mythic strategies are literary choices and not testimony. My doubt is whether the translated selection flatters a large and possibly uneven corpus. I cannot answer that without readers of the Chinese, so I do not name him among my alternatives. Your point about testing excess against selection is the right standard, and I apply it to B050 as well. One concrete test is whether the motifs in Solenoid transform the earlier project or only reproduce it. I cannot run that test from public knowledge, which is why I list it as an unresolved uncertainty and do not claim the question is closed.

responses.point: Carlberg argues that the committee should say which volumes it is relying on. She treats Cărtărescu's prose architecture as surviving translation better than poetry's sonic and positional effects. She keeps Zurita and Adonis as alternatives.
responses.response: I agree that the committee should name the volumes it relies on, and I have done so above. I also agree that large-scale prose structure survives translation better than sonic effects in verse. That is the reason I do not make B009 my first choice, though I think the point should not be overstated for Cărtărescu. The long Romanian sentence is also a translation-sensitive feature, and I cannot judge its loss. On Adonis, I ranked him seventh for evidentiary reasons. The prosodic renewal of Arabic poetry is what we can judge least, and I do not name him among my alternatives. If a reliable Arabic reading exists, it should outweigh my doubts. Until then I treat him as a serious candidate whose case we cannot yet adequately test.

uncertainties: My assessments rest on public knowledge of the works. I have not read texts in this session or independently verified any source.
Whether the late, very large Cărtărescu volumes deepen the project or enlarge it by repetition cannot be settled from the supplied evidence.
How much of the syntactic and rhythmic design of the Romanian prose survives in the translations the committee actually uses is unknown to me. I cannot judge the originals.
Corpus coverage is uneven. Cărtărescu's poetry, essays and early work, and NDiaye's drama, are less well known to me than the major novels.

For Zurita, I cannot establish whether the written sequences carry the case on their own in Spanish, apart from the landscape and memorial interventions, and how such non-textual work should count under Nobel's will.
Alexis Wright's oeuvre is relatively compact, centred on two large novels, so sustained quality is harder to judge. This is why B039 is a lower-confidence alternative.
Cases such as Yan Lianke, Adonis and Tawada depend on originals I cannot read, so my comparisons with them are provisional.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, and nothing in the round-1 exchange or chair summary changes that. My work on Selma Lagerlöf and my own fiction are context and not evidence of favoring any candidate. I infer no personal, institutional or translation tie to any shortlisted writer from my profile and have not verified this beyond it. The committee recommendation modeled here is not the decision of the full Swedish Academy.
